hero.title: Systems N#: a CLR perf lane where every cost is something you say out loud
hero.lede: You already know how to write fast code. What you don't have on the CLR is a compiler that *checks* the cost model and *explains* it. Systems N# is the same language and the same C# interop with a strict effect analyzer: `[hot]` means no hidden allocation, boxing, closure, or virtual dispatch — and the analyzer proves it at build time, names the exact NSYS### cost when you slip, and now emits `System.Numerics.Vector<T>` for the counted loops RyuJIT leaves scalar. Honest framing up front: it ties C# on the non-vectorizable kernels, beats C# ~2–6x on the vectorizable ones post-SIMD, and still trails Rust/C — within 2.02x at 4096, worst small-input cell 2.49x. That last gap is RyuJIT-vs-LLVM codegen, not anything N#-specific. This is not Rust on the CLR. Measured Apple M4, .NET 10, re-run 2026-06-07.

pillars.title: The effect model: [hot]/[boundary] and the NSYS### cost family
pillars.opinion: CLR costs should be visible, checkable, and explainable — not folklore you carry in your head.
pillars.body: `[hot]` is a contract: steady-state code with no allocation, boxing, closure/delegate construction, virtual dispatch, reflection, or throwing. `[boundary]` is the seam where setup may allocate and rent pools. Every hidden cost gets its own diagnostic — NSYS010 alloc, NSYS020 boxing, NSYS030 closure/delegate, NSYS040 virtual dispatch, NSYS060 AOT/trim blocker, NSYS080 lifetime/ref escape, NSYS100 ungoverned unsafe, NSYS160 dropped must-use Result — so the message tells you exactly what the hot path did wrong. When a `[hot]` function calls a cold callee that allocates, the analyzer follows the path and reports at the call site with the full chain (`ParseFrame -> DecodePayload -> FormatError`). Cost does not hide behind a function boundary. When a cost is deliberate, waive it in source with an auditable `allow(...)` recording reason and owner.

pillars.title: Result<T,E>: allocation-free structured errors, must-use
pillars.opinion: The success path should never pay for an exception, and a Result you forgot to check is a bug the compiler should catch.
pillars.body: `Result<T,E>` is a compiler-known `readonly struct` — a tag byte plus ok/err payloads, zero heap allocation on success or failure. Construct with `Ok(...)`/`Err(...)`, branch on `IsOk`/`IsErr`, read with `OkValueUnchecked`/`ErrValueUnchecked` once you've checked the tag. It is *must-use*: dropping one as a bare statement is NSYS160. If you really mean to ignore it, discard explicitly with `_ =`. A CLR exception is only ever paid if you choose to convert an `Err` into a throw. (General `value union` types are deferred; `Result<T,E>` is the one union that ships today.)

pillars.title: alloc and stackalloc: allocation you say out loud, stack spans without unsafe
pillars.opinion: Heap allocation should be a keyword you have to write, not a side effect you discover in a profiler.
pillars.body: The `alloc` keyword marks a heap allocation site so it's greppable and reviewable — allocation becomes a thing you say out loud. `stackalloc` gives you a `Span<T>` on the stack with no `unsafe` block. The length is bounded by `language.systems.stackBudgetBytes` (default 4096); blowing the budget is NSYS080. A stack span has `local` lifetime and physically cannot escape its frame — returning one is a compile error, not a dangling pointer. The memory story isn't "N# allocates less" on a pure i32 loop (it doesn't differ from C# or Rust — all stack/registers). It's the cost model: a naive `.Where(...).Select(...).Count()` allocates per element/per stage, while the `[hot]` span loop allocates *zero* and NSYS010 proves it at build time.

pillars.title: ref struct + spans + compile-time lifetimes
pillars.opinion: Zero-copy parsing should be ref-safe by construction — and we'll be honest that this is CLR escape analysis, not a borrow checker.
pillars.body: Zero-copy parsing leans on `ref struct` types and spans, with lifetimes checked at compile time. Ref-like fields live only in a `ref struct`; by-ref parameters are `&T`; you annotate parameter and return lifetimes with `scoped` and `returns 'a` to tie a returned slice to its backing buffer. The compiler computes a return-lifetime fact for every function (`local`, `param`, `heap(owner)`, `static`, or `unknown`) and rejects an `unknown` lifetime flowing into a `[hot]` caller. Be honest about scope: this is a CLR ref-safety model targeting the v1 escape shapes — it catches stack/span escapes. It is *not* a Rust borrow checker; move/affine ownership is deferred.

pillars.title: Restricted unsafe + [trusted(...)] governance
pillars.opinion: Unsafe code is fine — but it should carry its reason, owner, reviewer, and expiry, and be auditable from the CLI.
pillars.body: `unsafe { }` works in any project. In *systems* code it must live inside a function marked `[memory(safe)]` (you assert the public behavior is safe) and governed by `[trusted(...)]` recording **why** it's safe, **who** owns it, when it was **reviewed**, and when that sign-off **expires**. Without that governance the `unsafe` is NSYS100 — it fails the build. `nlc query trusted` reports every governed wrapper with owner, review date, expiry, body size, and callers, so trusted code is auditable across the whole codebase and sign-offs can't silently rot. Scope is intentionally narrow: function pointers, `fixed`/native interop, and pointer ops inside trusted wrappers — arbitrary pointer arithmetic is not in this version.

pillars.title: Auto-vectorization: the SIMD RyuJIT won't emit for you
pillars.opinion: If LLVM vectorizes your reduction and RyuJIT doesn't, that's the compiler's job to fix — not yours to hand-roll.
pillars.body: RyuJIT does not auto-vectorize counted reduction loops (LLVM does — that was the *entire* Rust/C gap on those kernels). So the N# IL backend recognizes the canonical hot-loop shapes and emits unrolled `System.Numerics.Vector<T>` directly: counted reductions (`for i<len { acc = acc + a[i] }`), range-predicate counts (`for i<len { if a[i] >= lo && a[i] <= hi count++ }`), a fused single-pass `Vector.Min`/`Vector.Max` for min/max reductions, and a seeded shifted-compare for adjacent-transition counts. On by default; set `NSHARP_VECTORIZE_REDUCTIONS=0` to opt out. Guards are conservative: unchecked context, exact element-type match, distinct accumulator/array/index names, and a side-effect-free bound. Measured (Apple M4, .NET 10, BenchmarkDotNet vs C# scalar, re-run 2026-06-07): checksum 4096 — C# 982.916ns vs N# 222.625ns (**4.4x faster**); count-ascii 4096 — C# 1174.088ns vs N# 298.051ns (**3.9x faster**); min-max-delta 4096 — C# 1496.034ns vs N# 253.578ns (**5.9x faster**); count-transitions 4096 — C# 1069.094ns vs N# 477.331ns (**2.2x faster**). The genuinely non-vectorizable kernel (rolling-hash, a carried dependency) correctly stays scalar at ~1.0x C#. FP reductions are deliberately excluded — FP addition isn't associative.

pillars.title: The CLI cost surface: ask the compiler what it costs
pillars.opinion: An LLM navigating your code should have the same cost X-ray a human gets — so the cost model is a queryable artifact, not a vibe.
pillars.body: The cost model isn't trapped in the analyzer; it's queryable and versioned. `nlc check --systems-report` emits canonical, schema-versioned JSON of every effect site. `nlc build --perf-report` is the deterministic allocation/dispatch/boxing/pool/trusted/AOT report. `nlc query perf --file Program.nl --pos 12:8` explains the cost facts at an exact position for a human or an LLM. `nlc query trusted` lists every governed `[trusted]` wrapper. This is the LLM-first half of the systems lane: the same answers VS Code shows you are available on the command line, stable across schema versions, so tooling can be built on top.
pillars.code:
$ nlc check --systems-report          # versioned JSON of every effect site
$ nlc build --perf-report             # alloc / dispatch / boxing / pool / trusted / AOT
$ nlc query perf --file Program.nl --pos 12:8   # explain costs at a position
$ nlc query trusted                   # audit every governed [trusted] wrapper

pillars.title: AOT and trimming: target-qualified facts, honestly scoped
pillars.opinion: AOT-readiness is a build-time correctness gate worth enforcing — and we won't pretend we emit a native image when we don't.
pillars.body: Under `aotTarget: nativeaot`, the analyzer reports per-symbol `aotSafe`/`trimSafe` facts and flags blockers as NSYS060, and `nlc publish` annotates `[RequiresUnreferencedCode]`/`[RequiresDynamicCode]` where appropriate. The honesty bar matters here: this is analysis-only today. `nlc publish` verifies AOT-safety and emits a normal framework-dependent assembly — it does *not* yet produce a native image (reports always set `nativeImageEmitted: false`). Treat AOT as a readiness/correctness gate, not native-image production. A full LLVM/NativeAOT-class backend remains on the performance backlog, not shipped.
pillars.code:
language:
  profile: systems
  systems:
    mode: strict          # effect violations are build-blocking errors
    aotTarget: nativeaot  # qualifies aotSafe/trimSafe facts; blockers => NSYS060
    stackBudgetBytes: 4096

closing: **Where N# stands today, measured (Apple M4, .NET 10, re-run 2026-06-07).** Systems N# is top-of-class among CLR languages: it ties C# (RyuJIT) within noise everywhere it isn't vectorizing, which makes routing a compiler hot path from C# to N# performance-neutral — the whole point of the cost model is that you get the safety and the X-ray without giving up speed. On the loops RyuJIT leaves scalar, the SIMD codegen pulls ahead of the C# baseline: ~4.4x on checksum reductions, ~3.9x on range-predicate counts, ~5.9x on the fused min/max-delta, ~2.2x on adjacent-transition counts (all at 4096 i32, measured vs the C# scalar baseline). It still **trails Rust and C** — from ~1.4x on the latency-bound rolling-hash floor up to 2.02x at 4096, with the worst single cell anywhere (min-max-delta at 64 elements, where fixed SIMD setup dominates) at 2.49x. Read that gap correctly: 100% of it is RyuJIT-vs-LLVM codegen quality, not anything N#-specific (N# ties C# everywhere it isn't vectorizing). So this is **not** \"Rust on the CLR\" and not \"as fast as Rust\" — it's a CLR language that makes allocation, dispatch, lifetimes, and memory safety *visible and checkable*, and closes the worst auto-vectorization gap from ~10.5x to within ~2x of native. Caveats worth stating out loud: a single ARM/M4 machine, mixed instruments (BenchmarkDotNet for N#/C# vs hand-rolled micro-benches for Rust/C), and six narrow synthetic i32 kernels — not a representative application. The honest claim is the load-bearing one: ties C#, beats it where it vectorizes, trails native on codegen, and tells you the truth about every cost in between."
